design_detail: One-page opinion column ('world view') in Nature Human Behaviour by a single author, Carl L. Hart, arguing that viewing drug use and addiction as a brain disease sustains unrealistic, costly and discriminatory drug policies. No methods, no data, no figures and no reference list: every number is stated without a source; the only sources named are two web addresses (the ABCD study; a Meth Project television advertisement) and a Newsweek quotation of 16 June 1986.
can_establish: What the author, a neuroscientist who studies drug effects in people, argues: that most people who take recreational drugs never become addicted, that no biological marker separates people with and without addiction, and that the brain-disease framing has helped justify harsh and racially unequal drug policies.
cannot_establish: Any of its figures (how few people who use a drug become addicted, the share of addiction explained by psychiatric and socioeconomic factors, the arrest and sentencing statistics), because none is sourced; or that the brain-disease view caused the policies described, which is argued by example, not shown.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (opinion piece). No studies are cited (p. 1).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: None stated; the piece has no reference list.
sample.selection_effects: Evidence selection is entirely the author's. The premises are presented as what he learned in more than 25 years of studying neuroscience (p. 1, 1st paragraph) and from his own community and family (9th paragraph); no counter-evidence is presented.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable. The piece concerns drug use and addiction in general, with examples for cocaine and crack cocaine, cannabis and methamphetamine (p. 1).

comparison.controls: Not applicable. The implied comparison is with Huntington's and Parkinson's disease, in which, the author says, examining an affected person's brain allows accurate predictions about the disease and its symptoms (p. 1, 2nd paragraph).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable. The author asserts, without data, that co-occurring psychiatric disorders and socioeconomic factors account for a substantial proportion of addictions (p. 1, 1st paragraph).

outcomes.operationalization: Addiction is not defined. A brain disease is defined by analogy: one in which looking at the brain of an affected person predicts the disease and its symptoms (p. 1, 2nd paragraph).

analysis.effect_sizes: None. Figures stated without sources: cannabis possession accounts for nearly half of the 1.5 million annual US drug arrests; Black people are four times more likely than white people to be arrested for cannabis possession although both groups use cannabis at similar rates (5th paragraph); a 1986 US law set penalties 100 times harsher for crack than for powder cocaine; more than 80% of people sentenced for crack cocaine offences are Black although most people who use the drug are white (8th paragraph) (all p. 1).
analysis.selective_reporting: No evidence for or against the brain-disease view is described; the piece does not mention, let alone answer, the findings its proponents cite.

interpretation_gap.results_show: The piece contains no results. It states, without sources or numbers, that cocaine and other recreational drugs temporarily alter specific neurons in everyone who takes them, that the vast majority of people who use them never become addicted, that co-occurring psychiatric disorders and socioeconomic factors account for a substantial proportion of the addictions that do occur, and that no biological substrate distinguishing people with and without addiction has been identified (p. 1, 1st paragraph).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The standfirst says the brain-disease view of drug use and addiction serves to perpetuate unrealistic, costly and discriminatory drug policies; the text calls the notion "catchy but empty" (p. 1, 2nd paragraph) and says human data showing addiction to be a brain disease, in the way Huntington's or Parkinson's disease are, are virtually absent. 'Vast majority' and 'relatively small percentage' are never quantified. The statement that the brains of people with and without addiction cannot be told apart is not distinguished from the weaker statement that no brain measure diagnoses an individual: group-level differences, which another paper in this batch mentions (Heyman, 2013, p. 34: DSM criteria separate groups by neural activity, citing Volkow et al., 1997), would contradict the first but not the second. The causal link between scientific framing and policy (the 1986 crack law, unequal arrests, the Meth Project advertisement, a 1986 Newsweek quotation) is argued by historical example, not tested.

timeline.event: US survey estimates of how many people who ever used each drug class became dependent (Anthony et al., 1994; project record, not read for this card): the kind of primary source the 'vast majority never become addicted' premise needs.

NESARC analysis of the probability of transition from first use to dependence on nicotine, alcohol, cannabis and cocaine (Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011; project record and card, not read for this card).

Critical review of cognitive functioning in people who use methamphetamine, led by Hart; the 2020 companion piece cites it for the absence of an identified neurobiological substrate of addiction (not read for this card).

Review of US national surveys: most people who had ever met criteria for drug dependence did not meet them in the past year (76% to 83% in the three later surveys), usually without treatment; it also notes that DSM criteria separate groups by neural activity (p. 34).

Volkow, Koob and McLellan's New England Journal of Medicine review of neurobiological advances from the brain disease model of addiction, the view Hart disputes; quoted in Hart (2020, p. 217); no project record.

Hart's Neuron essay restates the argument, calls this piece an open letter to NIDA, and gives a figure: 70% to 90% of people who use heroin or methamphetamine do not meet criteria for a substance use disorder, cited to his 2013 book.

replication.where_it_stands: The column is an argument, not evidence. Its central premises need primary sources: for how many people who use a drug become addicted, population surveys of transition from first use to dependence (records exist for Anthony et al., 1994, and Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011); for 'no biological substrate', neither Hart piece cites a study other than Hart et al. (2012), whose title concerns cognition in people who use methamphetamine. The policy and enforcement figures need official statistics.

funding.declared_conflicts: The author declares no competing interests (p. 1, Competing interests).
funding.affiliations_note: Carl L. Hart, Dirk Ziff Professor and Chair of the Department of Psychology and Professor in the Department of Psychiatry, Columbia University (p. 1). Hart runs human laboratory studies of drug effects; in the 2020 companion piece he names NIDA as his primary research funder (Hart, 2020, p. 216). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the argument.

what_would_settle_it: For the share of people who use a drug who become addicted: nationally representative surveys reporting, for each drug, how many people who ever used it ever met criteria for a use disorder, with the definition and time frame stated. For 'no biological marker': prospective studies testing whether any brain measure, taken before or during use, tells individuals with and without a use disorder apart better than chance in independent samples. For the policy claim: studies relating how addiction is framed by scientists to policy and enforcement outcomes.

domains.note: No search, no criteria and no reference list.
No study is cited, so none is appraised; every figure is given without a source.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: None of the author's studies is cited, but the key premises are presented as what he learned from his own research career (p. 1, 1st paragraph), so they rest on his judgment rather than on evidence shown in the piece.
Unsourced statements of fact (percentages, arrest ratios), personal experience and opinion are interleaved; causal statements about policy are made as facts.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on the brain-disease model of addiction
domains.note: Only the case against the model is presented; the evidence its proponents cite is neither described nor answered.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to an opinion piece (METHODS §5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is used. The column presents an argument without a search, sources or appraisal, and its figures are unsourced. It may be cited for what Carl Hart argues and as a pointer to the debate, not as evidence for any figure: claims about how many people who use drugs become addicted, or about arrest and sentencing disparities, need primary sources.

key_findings.finding: The author argues that the view of drug use and addiction as a brain disease serves to perpetuate unrealistic, costly and discriminatory drug policies, and calls for 'neuro-exaggerations' to stop determining research funding, views on drugs and drug policies.

He states, without a source or a number, that cocaine and other recreational drugs temporarily alter the functioning of specific neurons in everyone who takes them, yet the vast majority of people who use them never become addicted; and that among the relatively small percentage who do, co-occurring psychiatric disorders and socioeconomic factors account for a substantial proportion of the addictions.

He states that no biological substrate differentiating people with addiction from people without it has been identified, that there are virtually no human data showing addiction to be a brain disease in the way Huntington's or Parkinson's disease are (where the brain predicts the disease and its symptoms), and that researchers are nowhere near able to tell the brains of people with and without addiction apart; no study is cited.

He argues that if addiction is located in the interaction of drug and brain, policy is left with two options, removing the drug from society through law enforcement or focusing only on the individual's brain, with no interest in socioeconomic factors; he gives the multimillion-dollar Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study, which mainly gathers neuroimaging data, as an example of funding with no equivalent for psychosocial determinants.
key_findings.locator: 3rd paragraph (left column, continuing in the middle column) and 4th paragraph (middle column)

key_findings.finding: Enforcement figures stated without sources: millions are arrested each year for drug possession; in the United States cannabis possession accounts for nearly half of the 1.5 million annual drug arrests, and Black people are four times more likely than white people to be arrested for it although both groups use cannabis at similar rates.

He says the diseased-brain view treats any use of certain drugs as pathological, although non-problematic recreational use characterizes the experience of the overwhelming majority who take them; his example is a US anti-drug television advertisement implying that one hit of methamphetamine causes irrevocable damage.

On crack cocaine in the 1980s: addiction was said to follow a single hit and drug experts with neuroscience leanings were quoted in the press (a Yale psychiatry professor in Newsweek, 16 June 1986); in 1986 the US Congress set penalties 100 times harsher for crack than for powder cocaine, and more than 80% of people sentenced for crack offences are Black although most people who use the drug are white (no sources given).
key_findings.locator: 7th paragraph (middle column, continuing in the right column) and 8th paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: He states that the scientific community has virtually ignored racial discrimination in drug-law enforcement and that the researchers themselves are overwhelmingly white and do not live with the consequences of their work.
The piece has no reference list; its only sources are two web addresses and one magazine quotation.

reporting_issues.issue: Every number in the piece (1.5 million arrests, nearly half for cannabis possession, four times the arrest rate, penalties 100 times harsher, more than 80% of crack sentences) is given without a source, and there is no reference list.
reporting_issues.consequence: None of these figures can be checked from the piece; any claim using them must cite the primary statistics.

reporting_issues.issue: The proportions on which the argument turns ('vast majority' never addicted; 'relatively small percentage' addicted; 'substantial proportion' explained by psychiatric and socioeconomic factors) are not quantified, and the drugs and populations meant are not specified beyond cocaine and other recreational drugs.
reporting_issues.consequence: The piece cannot support a number for how many people who use a drug become addicted. The companion piece gives 70% to 90% not meeting criteria for a use disorder, cited only to the author's 2013 book (Hart, 2020, p. 216).

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record), p. 1 (the whole one-page article, Nature Human Behaviour 1, article number 0055; read on the rendered page; the piece has no reference list; no supplement). Paragraphs are counted through the whole piece, which has no section headings (10 paragraphs).
